title: Pentagon UFO Files 2026: Pentagon UFO Files Reveal a 1956 Encounter That Lasted Minutes - The Pilot Saw Something Strange, But Other Radar Systems Saw Nothing
excerpt: Pentagon UFO Files 2026: Pentagon UFO files reveal a proposed underground vault, Cold War fighter encounters and mysterious radar detections as the latest US government release revisits decades of UAP investigations.
content:
Pentagon UFO Files 2026: A buried vault in Nevada, a fighter pilot chasing an unidentified radar signal and decades-old reports of strange objects in the sky might sound like scenes from a science-fiction film. But all three appear in a newly released collection of US government records that offers a rare look at how officials documented and examined unexplained aerial incidents.

The Pentagon released 43 new files on November 20 as part of its latest release of Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena (UAP) records. The collection contains 40 documents and three military videos, bringing together material from different periods, including Cold War-era reports and more recent sensor detections.

One of the most striking documents is a 538-page report prepared in 2009 by Bigelow Aerospace Advanced Space Studies (BAASS). It described plans for a secure underground facility in North Las Vegas that could hold biological samples, unidentified hardware and what the report called “exotic material or tissue.”

However, the records do not prove that BAASS possessed alien material or that the proposed vault was ever constructed. There is no public record showing that the facility was built.

Pentagon UFO Files 2026: 2009 Report Described a Heavily Secured Underground Vault

The BAASS report proposed placing the facility 15 to 20 feet below the ground at the company’s North Las Vegas premises.

The planned storage area would cover about 5,000 square feet and feature walls around three feet thick. The design also called for a heavy steel door and camouflage for any part of the structure that could remain visible above ground.

The report said BAASS wanted a secure location because it might obtain unusual material or biological samples from private individuals, research groups and other sources, including Brazil.

It stated that the company lacked a suitable secure facility to store “exotic material or tissue” that it could potentially acquire.

That language has attracted attention because of the long-running association between BAASS and US government-funded research into UAPs. But the document describes a proposal and anticipated acquisitions, not a confirmed recovery operation.

Pentagon UFO Files 2026: Cold War-Era UFO Reports Reappear in the Files

The latest release also takes readers back to the 1950s, when US military and intelligence agencies regularly investigated reports of unusual objects and lights.

One file concerns Clarence “Kelly” Johnson, the famous Lockheed engineer associated with aircraft such as the U-2 and SR-71.

According to the record, Johnson reported seeing a dark, elliptical object hovering against the sunset near his California ranch in 1953. He reportedly watched it through binoculars for several minutes before it moved away.

Another Lockheed test crew also reportedly saw a large flying-wing-shaped object around the same period.

But an Air Force assessment later identified Johnson’s sighting as a lenticular cloud, showing that at least one of the unusual reports eventually received a conventional explanation.

Pentagon UFO Files 2026: Fighter Pilot Reported Strange Radar Contact Over Japan

Another file describes a much more unusual encounter involving a US Air Force F-86D fighter near Ube, Japan, in December 1956.

Two pilots from the 68th Fighter-Interceptor Squadron were conducting practice intercepts when one pilot detected another radar target.

The radar return reportedly remained visible for seven to eight minutes. The pilot later reported intermittent visual contact and described the object as resembling the upper half of a sphere.

He tried to close the distance but could not get closer than about five nautical miles. The report estimated that the object moved away at between 1,500 and 1,800 knots.

There was a major complication: neither the second aircraft nor ground-based radar detected the same object. The historical report therefore recorded the encounter without providing a conclusive identification.

Pentagon UFO Files 2026: New Files Also Include Modern Radar Detections

The release is not limited to stories from the early days of the Cold War.

One of the newer records concerns radar detections recorded in 2023. According to reports examining the released material, eight detections appeared over a period of about 84 seconds at altitudes between 55,000 and 70,000 feet.

If all eight detections represented one continuous object, the calculated average ground speed would have been around 1,650 mph.

But the available information does not establish that a single object produced all eight radar tracks. That distinction is important because the release documents an unresolved detection rather than confirming the presence of an extraordinary aircraft.

Pentagon UFO Files 2026: What About the Nimitz and Lakenheath Cases?

The broader collection also connects with some of the best-known US and UK military UAP investigations.

The records include material linked to the 2004 USS Nimitz encounter and the reported 2007 incident involving US F-15C pilots near RAF Lakenheath in Britain.

These cases have attracted years of public attention because they involved military personnel and aircraft rather than only civilian eyewitnesses.

The newly released material adds to the historical record but does not turn those incidents into confirmed evidence of extraterrestrial spacecraft.

Pentagon UFO Files 2026: Pentagon Files Do Not Confirm Aliens

The biggest takeaway from the new release may be what the documents do not establish.

The files show that US government agencies and military personnel investigated reports involving strange objects, unusual radar returns and unexplained aerial activity. Some cases received possible conventional explanations, while others remained unresolved because investigators lacked enough information to identify what witnesses or sensors recorded.

The Pentagon’s latest UAP releases therefore offer more evidence of government investigations than evidence of extraterrestrial visitors. The files document uncertainty, competing explanations and unanswered questions rather than a definitive discovery of alien life.

As the US continues releasing UAP records in batches, the latest documents provide another snapshot of a decades-old mystery — one that now includes everything from Cold War fighter encounters to a proposed underground vault designed to protect material that investigators hoped they might someday recover.
